query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: An integrated experimental–computational framework that combines rapid DSC measurements, in‐situ neutron imaging, and atomistic MD simulations calibrated via CALPHAD will accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, volume change at melting, and selected liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the high‐entropy alloy family.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys in fully solid-solution states (both single-crystalline and polycrystalline forms, e.g., equiatomic compositions such as CoCrFeMnNi or refractory systems like NbMoTaWV) at ambient temperature.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled heating experiments using DSC across a wide temperature range up to the solidus/melting point together with simultaneous in-situ neutron imaging to record density/volume changes. Complement these measurements with calibrated MD simulations (using potentials like 2NN MEAM) refined through CALPHAD thermodynamic descriptions.
generation.conditions: Heating at controlled rates (e.g., 10 K increments with relaxation steps) under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation; use of appropriately sized samples for both DSC and neutron imaging; simulations carried out over a temperature range spanning from room temperature to above the experimentally determined melting point.
generation.structural_mediator: Local atomic rearrangements and emerging short-range order (observed via MD simulation) that correlate with macroscopic density changes and phase transitions captured by neutron imaging and DSC.
generation.mechanism: The DSC yields precise heat capacity curves and endothermic/exothermic peaks corresponding to fusion and phase transitions. When directly correlated with in-situ neutron imaging, which captures abrupt density changes and liquid phase miscibility phenomena, and with MD simulation outputs that provide atomistic insight into enthalpy and local ordering effects, the integrated data allow extraction of fusion enthalpy, entropy and volume changes. CALPHAD modeling is used to validate and bridge scales between simulation and experiment.
generation.predicted_outcome: The integrated approach will produce measurements of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, and volume change at melting with quantitative accuracy within roughly 5–10% compared to benchmark standards. Liquid-phase thermodynamic properties will also be determined with similar precision, and the approach will reveal consistent correlations across different crystallographic phases and grain sizes.
generation.baseline: Traditional DSC and calorimetry experiments separately combined with independent MD simulations. Existing approaches that use either experimental or computational methods in isolation.
generation.boundary: The method is expected to work for HEAs that exhibit clearly detectable DSC peaks and sufficient neutron contrast in the liquid state. Its performance may be limited in alloys with extremely sluggish kinetics, very weak DSC signals, or where neutron attenuation differences are too small to distinguish phase separation.
generation.uncertainty: While DSC and MD simulation methods have been applied separately in studies such as PMC7513177 and PMC8956691, and neutron imaging has been successfully used (PMC8320920), the proposed combination has not been demonstrated. Uncertainties lie in the alignment of time scales between the rapid DSC-neutron experiments and the simulation evolution, and in achieving robust calibration across disparate materials systems without introducing significant systematic errors.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a benchmark equiatomic HEA (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) and perform simultaneous DSC and in-situ neutron imaging while running MD simulations calibrated via CALPHAD. Compare the measured melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, and volume change at melting against independently obtained high-resolution experimental measurements (e.g., from calorimetry and diffraction studies).
measurements: DSC-based heat capacity and enthalpy curves
Neutron imaging radiographs to extract density/volume change profiles
MD simulation outputs of energy change and local ordering
Benchmark thermodynamic property data from literature or standardized experiments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integrated framework produces fusion thermodynamic parameters that deviate by more than approximately 10% from the independently benchmarked values, or if the correlations between DSC peaks, imaging density shifts, and atomistic simulation predictions do not consistently align across sample types and heating rates, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractWe determined the entropy of high entropy alloys by investigating single-crystalline nickel and five high entropy alloys: two fcc-alloys, two bcc-alloys and one hcp-alloy. Since the configurational entropy of these single-phase alloys differs from alloys using a base element, it is important to quantify the entropy. Using differential scanning calorimetry, cp-measurements are carried out from −170 °C to the materials’ solidus temperatures TS. From these experiments, we determined the thermal entropy and compared it to the configurational entropy for each of the studied alloys. We applied the rule of mixture to predict molar heat capacities of the alloys at room temperature, which were in good agreement with the Dulong-Petit law. The molar heat capacity of the studied alloys was about three times the universal gas constant, hence the thermal entropy was the major contribution to total entropy. The configurational entropy, due to the chemical composition and number of components, contributes less on the absolute scale. The field of high-entropy alloys continues to grow every year, and with this growth comes an enormous amount of never before seen alloy systems with unknown liquid state behavior. As previously shown, neutron imaging can be a very useful technique to elucidate the liquid state behavior of molten alloy systems. With the application of this technique to high-entropy alloys, in-situ imaging of liquid state miscibility has been observed for the first time with the equiatomic additions of Ni to the immiscible CoCrCu system. The current results show the following: Neutron imaging can be utilized to image liquid state behavior in high-entropy alloys. Imaging was carried out on equiatomic CoCrCu buttons with equiatomic additions of Ni such that when melting occurred between the alloying elements, full miscibility was achieved. In-situ neutron imaging was successfully utilized to image in-situ alloying of Ni into an immiscible CoCrCu system. The synthesis of the CoCrCuNi alloy inside the high-temperature furnace was fully imaged via a movie-like sequence of carefully timed radiographs to display the melting/alloying process. The melting mechanism of single crystal and polycrystalline Nb20.6Mo21.7Ta15.6W21.1V21.0 refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) were investigated by the molecular dynamics (MD) simulation using the second-nearest neighbor modified embedded-atom method (2NN MEAM) potential. For the single crystal RHEA, the density profile displays an abrupt drop from 11.25 to 11.00 g/cm3 at temperatures from 2910 to 2940 K, indicating all atoms begin significant local structural rearrangement. For polycrystalline RHEAs, a two-stage melting process is found. In the first melting stage, the melting of the grain boundary (GB) regions firstly occurs at the pre-melting temperature, which is relatively lower than the corresponding system-melting point. At the pre-melting temperature, most GB atoms have enough kinetic energies to leave their equilibrium positions, and then gradually induce the rearrangement of grain atoms close to GB. In the second melting stage at the melting point, most grain atoms have enough kinetic energies to rearrange, resulting in the chemical short-ranged order changes of all pairs.
